newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax deal distant, industry slams reforms.
newsitem.headline: German tax deal distant, industry slams reforms.

text.p: As German government and opposition politicians on Tuesday ended talks over planned tax reforms without result, an impressive line-up of industry heavyweights slammed the tax plans as bad for investment.

Politicians from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) met the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to begin talking about a compromise on tax reforms.

Tax bills for 1998 and 1999 were defeated last week in the upper house, which is controlled by the opposition, after it had gained passage in the lower house with a majority vote by deputies from Kohl's coalition.
German industry leaders said the tax package was creating fresh uncertainty rather than a favourable climate for business and having a negative impact on investment and jobs.

"The latest tax reform plans of the government coalition clearly burden industry," William Boddie, chairman Ford Motor Co's German subsidiary Ford-Werke AG, told the monthly magazine Impulse. "It appears as though business will finance the lion's share of the tax reform."

The lower house of parliament last week passed two bills, which contain a package of income tax cuts of around 30 billion marks ($17.1 billion) over the next two years, but also contain changes to corporate taxes that lead to higher burdens in 1998.

The Federation of German Industry estimates companies will pay additional taxes of around 13.7 billion marks next year as a result of the reform and questions whether relief promised in 1999 will really be introduced after German elections in 1998.
The magazine carried critical comments from chief executives from chemical giant Bayer AG, utility RWE AG, steel and engineering group Thyssen AG, and media conglomerate Bertelsmann AG.
The heads of RWE and Thyssen both complained that laws changes to corporate taxes would particularly hit their companies.
One of the changes, restricting the way companies can carry forward losses from previous years to offset tax liability in profitable years, would hit cyclical industries like steel.

"The higher tax burden would seriously weaken our position in international competition which is already hard," said Thyssen chairman Dieter Vogel. "The pressure to rationalise would become greater, investments in Germany questioned."

Bertelsmann chairman Mark Woessner said the change in rules on losses carried forward would also hit new, start-up companies that must first get established on the market before they become profitable.
The tax reform would also force utilities to dissolve tax free reserves, piled up in past year in order to pay for decommissioning nuclear reactors.
"This latest Bonn tax farce robs us of our hopes for tax reform that is oriented towards the future," said Dietmar Kuhnt, chairman of RWE, Germany's biggest power utility.
"Instead of putting Germany in the fast lane of international competition, the skid-marks on labour policies from the latest tax proposals are already noticeable."
